lesson.title: Ort I: hier, dort, drüben, gegenüber, der Umweg
lesson.subtitle: the words that point — and the sound shift hiding inside dort

hook.title: English Points Twice, German Points Four Times
hook.content: English points with here and there and then gives up. German points four times. hier and here are the purest twins you will ever meet — both come from the same Proto-Germanic *hiar, untouched, with no shift to explain. dort is da wearing a pointing suffix — and da is there's plain twin: the same ancient adverb *þar, with German hardening the breathy th to d — the same law that made drei out of three and das out of that. drüben is über wearing its adverb coat — 'on the over side' — and über ↔ over is the V→B twin you know from geben/give. gegenüber stacks gegen ('against') on über ('over') — over-against — a relation English writes as a whole phrase. Der Umweg is um + Weg, a way-around, and Weg ↔ way is a twin as old as the road. So the honest score: English kept here and there, but lost drüben and gegenüber as single words and spells the detour with borrowed letters; German still runs three rungs of distance — hier, dort, drüben.

footnotes.title: The TH→D Family Reunion
footnotes.content: Once you hear TH→D you hear it everywhere: three/drei, that/das, thou/du, there/da — and dort is just da with the pointing suffix. One sound law, one family, thousands of years old — and German never stopped inviting the th to harden. Say da and there back to back and feel the d and the th be the same consonant wearing two dialects.

pattern.title: Four Words, Three Distances
pattern.content: 1. Here: Ich wohne hier — where you stand. 2. There: Die Brücke ist drüben — across the gap, visible but far. 3. Plain there: Das Auto ist dort. 4. Opposite: Gegenüber ist die Kirche — or with a noun, postposed: das Haus gegenüber. 5. The detour: Wir nehmen einen Umweg — 'a way around'. 6. Right away: Ich komme sofort. And the numbers still point: das Haus gegenüber hat die Nummer eins.
pattern.linguist_note: Three degrees of distance is the old Germanic system: hier, dort, drüben. English once had the third rung too — yonder, still alive in dialects — but standard English collapsed to two words and a phrase ('over there'). German never had to collapse; the system is intact.

exercises.prompt: The pointing words in place — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The house opposite has number one
matching_pairs.german: Das Haus gegenüber hat die Nummer eins

exercises.target_answer: Ich wohne hier, Die Brücke ist drüben, Gegenüber ist die Kirche, Das Haus gegenüber hat die Nummer eins, Wir nehmen einen Umweg, Ich komme sofort
exercises.meaning: here, over there, opposite, detour, right away
exercises.explanation: Notice the two faces of gegenüber: alone in position 1 (Gegenüber ist die Kirche) or trailing its noun (das Haus gegenüber). One word, two seats — and der Umweg is literally a 'way-around'.

exercises.prompt: dort ↔ there — which shift badge does the pair wear?
exercises.meaning: dort is there's twin: the ancient *þar with th hardened to d
exercises.explanation: Both point back to Proto-Germanic *þar. English kept the breathy th; German hardened it to d — the same law as drei/three and das/that. And you can see the V→B badge on the word drüben: über ↔ over, with b where English has v.

exercises.prompt: The purest twin in the lesson: hier. Spell its English twin — the one word that never shifted at all:
exercises.explanation: hier and here are the same Proto-Germanic word *hiar with no shift to explain — h stayed h, the vowel stayed itself. The twins never moved apart; the spelling just drifted one letter.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the detour sentence: 'We take a detour'
exercises.explanation: nehmen + einen Umweg — masculine accusative, the same case as einen Moment, bitte. The compound says exactly what it does: um + Weg, a way-around. Distractors wait in the bank, but the detour is the destination.
wohnen in slot 2, immer right behind it, hier at the end — the frequency adverb from the Wie-oft lesson doing its job in a new house. Swap hier for dort and the sentence moves across town.

summary.outcome: Point four ways — hier, dort, drüben, gegenüber — take an Umweg, and hear the TH→D shift inside dort.

use_example.german: Ich wohne hier — die Brücke ist drüben.
use_example.english: I live here — the bridge is over there.

summary.takeaway: hier/here never shifted, dort/there wears TH→D, drüben hides über/over, gegenüber is gegen+über stacked, and der Umweg is a 'way-around' — Weg and way are the same word.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Richtung I — links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten — the words that tell you which way.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Ort I: hier, dort, drüben, gegenüber, der Umweg (We always live here):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir wohnen immer hier" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Ort I: hier, dort, drüben, gegenüber, der Umweg without relying on short-term echo.

hier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hēr — the explicit cognate of English here. [wiktionary]

drüben.context_translation: The post office is over there.
drüben.etymology_derivation: From a rare üben, a variant of über formed by the analogy of unter/unten and ober/oben — literally over yonder; über is the twin of over. [wiktionary]

gegenüber.context_phrase: Der Supermarkt ist gegenüber der Bank.
gegenüber.context_translation: The supermarket is opposite the bank.
gegenüber.etymology_derivation: gegen + über — literally over-against; über is the twin of English over (both from PIE *upér) and gegen the twin of against. [wiktionary]

umweg.context_phrase: Wir nehmen einen Umweg wegen der Baustelle.
umweg.context_translation: We take a detour because of the construction site.
umweg.etymology_derivation: um + Weg, from Middle High German umbe, around, plus wec, way; Weg is the documented twin of way — an around-way, a detour. [wiktionary]

wohnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from the 'wish, love' root; no English cognate named on Wiktionary. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

kirche.etymology_derivation: Greek kyriakon → Scottish kirk / German Kirche.

brücke.context_phrase: Die alte Brücke ist aus Stein.
brücke.context_translation: The old bridge is made of stone.
brücke.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *bruggju — the page lists English bridge as the cognate; German keeps the hard k where English softened to dg. [wiktionary]

nummer.etymology_derivation: From Italian numero, from Latin numerus — the same Latin word that gives English number. [wiktionary]

eins.context_translation: I have only one of those.
eins.etymology_derivation: Contraction of eines, Proto-Germanic *ainaz — the twin of English one (see ein). [wiktionary]

immer.context_phrase: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen.
immer.context_translation: I always drink coffee in the morning.
immer.etymology_derivation: OHG iomēr 'ever + more' — cognate with Middle English 'a mare' (evermore). [wiktionary]

sofort.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German so vōrt — literally 'so forth', mirroring the English phrase. [wiktionary]

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

lebensmittel.context_translation: We buy groceries at the supermarket.
lebensmittel.etymology_derivation: Lebensmittel — Leben (life, cognate with live, whose v German closed to b) plus Mittel (means, cognate with middle via the d to t stop shift); literally means of life. [wiktionary]

deshalb.context_phrase: Es regnete, deshalb blieben wir zu Hause.
deshalb.context_translation: It rained, therefore we stayed at home.
deshalb.etymology_derivation: Des (genitive of das, twin of the/that) plus halb (side, half — twin of English half, where English f became German b); literally of that side, therefore. [wiktionary]

eben.context_translation: Just come along to the cinema.
eben.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, flat, even; the page lists English even as the direct cognate — the v closing to b in German. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
